warmup.q: A coroutine on Dispatchers.Default runs for (t in transactions) score(t) over two million transactions, with no suspend calls inside the loop. Another coroutine calls job.cancel() halfway through. What happens?
options: The loop stops at once, because cancel() stops the coroutine's thread
The loop stops at the next iteration, because the compiler adds a check to every loop
The loop runs to the end, and only then does the job finish as cancelled
cancel() throws IllegalStateException, because the coroutine is busy
warmup.why: Cancellation is cooperative. cancel() only marks the job as cancelling. The coroutine notices at its next suspension point or explicit check, and this loop has neither, so it finishes all two million transactions first. Java's Future.cancel(true) has the same limit: it sets a flag that someone has to read.

sections.h: Cancellation is a request your code has to notice
sections.html:
job.cancel() doesn't stop a coroutine. It marks the job as cancelling, and that's all. The coroutine stops the next time it reaches a suspension point that checks: delay, withContext, await, join, a channel's send or receive, yield. That call throws CancellationException, the exception unwinds the stack, finally blocks run, and the job ends as cancelled. A coroutine that is already suspended notices at once: one waiting in delay(10_000) is resumed with the exception straight away.

Code that never reaches such a point never notices. A CPU loop over two million card transactions runs to the end. So does a blocking call such as Thread.sleep or a JDBC query (section 4). This is cooperative cancellation. Java has the same model: Future.cancel(true) sets the interrupt flag, and a loop that never reads it keeps going.

A CPU loop cooperates by checking now and then:

Java
// Java equivalent: read the interrupt flag yourself
void scan(List<Txn> rows) {
    for (int i = 0; i < rows.size(); i++) {
        if (i % 1_000 == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) throw new CancellationException();
        score(rows.get(i));
    }
}
Kotlin
suspend fun scan(rows: List<Txn>) = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
    for ((i, row) in rows.withIndex()) {
        if (i % 1_000 == 0) ensureActive()   // throws CancellationException once cancelled
        score(row)
    }
}

You have three tools. ensureActive() throws if the job is cancelled. isActive returns a boolean, for loops that want to stop quietly: while (isActive) { ... }. yield() checks too, and also lets other coroutines waiting for the same dispatcher run, which matters when a long loop shares a small dispatcher. A check is just a read of the job's state, so it costs almost nothing, but once every few hundred rows is plenty.

Watch which job you are checking. Inside launch { }, isActive and ensureActive() refer to that coroutine. A plain suspend function has no scope receiver, so write currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive(). In a lambda nested inside another scope, a bare isActive can quietly refer to the outer scope.

Flow (lesson 7 of this track) has the same trap at a smaller scale. A flow { } builder checks on every emit, but asFlow() doesn't:

Java
// Java equivalent: a stream never reads the interrupt flag on its own
IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).forEach(i -> {
    if (i == 3) Thread.currentThread().interrupt();   // ask to stop
    System.out.println(i);                            // prints 1 to 5
});
Kotlin
(1..5).asFlow().collect { if (it == 3) cancel(); println(it) }                // prints 1 to 5
(1..5).asFlow().cancellable().collect { if (it == 3) cancel(); println(it) }  // prints 1 to 3

try.title: Cancel four CPU loops
steps: Read CancelABusyLoop.kt. Each loop would take about 1.5 s; the demo cancels it after 100 ms. Predict how long each one takes to stop.
Run it.
In the ensureActive() loop, change 1_000 to 10_000_000 and run it again. Predict first.
Run the Java twin, which uses Future.cancel(true) and the interrupt flag.

code.title: CancelABusyLoop.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l05 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.ensureActive import kotlinx.coroutines.isActive import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.yield /** Pure CPU work: a checksum over one fake card number. 60 million of them take about 1.5 s. */ private fun checksum(i: Long): Long { var x = i repeat(20) { x = x xor (x ushr 33) x *= -0xae502812aa7333L x = x xor (x ushr 29) } return x } private const val ROWS = 60_000_000L @Volatile private var sink = 0L // keeps the JIT from deleting loops whose result nobody reads fun main() = runBlocking { // each loop gets the launched coroutine as its receiver, so isActive and ensureActive() look at // that coroutine's job (in a plain lambda they would quietly pick up runBlocking's scope instead) val loops: Map<String, suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Long> = mapOf( "no check" to { var sum = 0L for (i in 0 until ROWS) sum += checksum(i) sum }, "while (isActive)" to { var sum = 0L var i = 0L while (isActive && i < ROWS) { sum += checksum(i); i++ } sum }, "ensureActive() every 1,000" to { var sum = 0L for (i in 0 until ROWS) { if (i % 1_000 == 0L) ensureActive() sum += checksum(i) } sum }, "yield() every 1,000" to { var sum = 0L for (i in 0 until ROWS) { if (i % 1_000 == 0L) yield() sum += checksum(i) } sum }, ) for ((label, loop) in loops) { val job = launch(Dispatchers.Default) { sink = loop() } delay(100) // let it get going val asked = System.nanoTime() job.cancelAndJoin() println("%-28s stopped %5d ms after cancel()".format(label, (System.nanoTime() - asked) / 1_000_000)) } }

alt.title: CancelABusyLoopJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of CancelABusyLoop.kt: Future.cancel(true) only sets the interrupt flag. // A CPU loop stops only if it looks at the flag. package workbench.coroutines.l05; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class CancelABusyLoopJava { static final long ROWS = 60_000_000L; static volatile long sink; // keeps the JIT from deleting loops whose result nobody reads /** Pure CPU work: a checksum over one fake card number. 60 million of them take about 1.5 s. */ static long checksum(long i) { long x = i; for (int k = 0; k < 20; k++) { x ^= x >>> 33; x *= -0xae502812aa7333L; x ^= x >>> 29; } return x; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Map<String, Runnable> loops = new LinkedHashMap<>(); loops.put("no check", () -> { long sum = 0; for (long i = 0; i < ROWS; i++) sum += checksum(i); sink = sum; }); loops.put("isInterrupted() every 1,000", () -> { long sum = 0; for (long i = 0; i < ROWS; i++) { if (i % 1_000 == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) break; sum += checksum(i); } sink = sum; }); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); // one thread, so the no-op below waits for it for (var e : loops.entrySet()) { Future<?> f = pool.submit(e.getValue()); Thread.sleep(100); // let it get going long asked = System.nanoTime(); f.cancel(true); // sets the interrupt flag; the future reports "cancelled" at once // wait for the thread itself to come back: the no-op runs only once the loop has stopped pool.submit(() -> { }).get(); System.out.printf("%-28s stopped %5d ms after cancel(true)%n", e.getKey(), (System.nanoTime() - asked) / 1_000_000); } pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } }

try.expect: The loop with no check stops about 1,000 ms after cancel() (or more on a slow machine): it simply finished its work. The other three stop within a few milliseconds. With a check only every 10 million rows, that loop stops late, at its next check (10 million rows take a couple of hundred ms). The Java twin shows the same split: cancel(true) reports success at once, but the loop that never reads the flag keeps its thread busy until it ends.

video.title: Cancellation is a request: a coroutine stops only at a suspension point or a check

sections.h: CancellationException carries the cancel, so never swallow it
sections.html:
Cancellation travels as an exception, CancellationException (on the JVM it is java.util.concurrent.CancellationException). That is the point of it: it unwinds the stack, runs every finally and closes every use. It is also the danger. Any catch that catches it stops it.

Java
// Java equivalent: swallowing InterruptedException
for (String id : batchIds) {
    try { settle(id); }
    catch (InterruptedException e) { log.warn("batch {} failed", id, e); failed.add(id); }  // the cancel request is gone
}
Kotlin
for (id in batchIds) {
    runCatching { settle(id) }                                   // also catches CancellationException
        .onFailure { log.warn("batch $id failed", it); failed += id }
}

runCatching catches every Throwable. So do catch (e: Exception) and catch (e: Throwable), because CancellationException extends IllegalStateException. Here is what happens when the pod shuts down and cancels this run. The batch in progress is logged as failed. The loop moves to the next batch, which starts, hits its first suspension point, throws at once and is logged as failed too, and so on to the end of the list. Then the function returns normally, with a list of "failed" batches that never failed. In a while (true) polling loop it is worse: every delay throws at once, the exception is swallowed, and the loop spins at full CPU forever.

The fix is to let it through. With runCatching, rethrow it first: .onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it; ... }. With try, put catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } before the general clause. Better still, catch only what you expect, such as IOException or your client's error type, and let everything else propagate.

The Java rule is the same: catch InterruptedException, restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt(), and stop. But the failure looks different, and the Try it shows how. A swallowed interrupt clears the flag, so the next sleep sleeps normally and the loop just runs to the end at its usual pace. A swallowed cancellation clears nothing. The job stays cancelled, every later suspension point throws at once, and the loop races to the end in a few milliseconds.

So a coroutine that is cancelled cannot be talked out of it. Catching the exception only means the code after the catch runs inside a coroutine that is still cancelled.

try.title: Swallow a cancel and count the damage
steps: Read SwallowedCancellation.kt. The poller is cancelled at 250 ms, after 3 attempts. Predict how many attempts run after the cancel, and how long cancelAndJoin takes.
Run it.
Run it with -Pargs=fixed, which rethrows CancellationException.
Run the Java twin both ways and compare how long shutdown takes.

code.title: SwallowedCancellation.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l05 import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException /** Polls a settlement 20 times, 100 ms apart. A failed poll is logged and retried. */ suspend fun pollSettlement(rethrowCancellation: Boolean, onAttempt: () -> Unit) { repeat(20) { runCatching { onAttempt() // the HTTP call to the acquirer would go here delay(100) }.onFailure { e -> if (rethrowCancellation && e is CancellationException) throw e // swallowed: logged as a "failed poll", and the loop goes round again } } } fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val fixed = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" var attempts = 0 var cancelledAt = -1 val poller = launch { pollSettlement(rethrowCancellation = fixed) { attempts++ } } delay(250) cancelledAt = attempts val asked = System.nanoTime() poller.cancelAndJoin() val ms = (System.nanoTime() - asked) / 1_000_000 println(if (fixed) "runCatching + rethrow:" else "runCatching, swallowing:") println(" attempts before cancel: $cancelledAt, after cancel: ${attempts - cancelledAt}, cancelAndJoin took $ms ms") }

alt.title: SwallowedCancellationJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of SwallowedCancellation.kt: catching InterruptedException and carrying on // swallows the cancel request, just as runCatching swallows CancellationException. package workbench.coroutines.l05; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; public class SwallowedCancellationJava { static void pollSettlement(boolean restoreInterrupt, AtomicInteger attempts) { for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) { try { attempts.incrementAndGet(); // the HTTP call to the acquirer would go here Thread.sleep(100); } catch (InterruptedException e) { if (restoreInterrupt) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return; // stop: somebody asked us to } // swallowed: the flag is now clear, so the next sleep() sleeps normally } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean fixed = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); AtomicInteger attempts = new AtomicInteger(); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); pool.submit(() -> pollSettlement(fixed, attempts)); Thread.sleep(250); int cancelledAt = attempts.get(); long asked = System.nanoTime(); pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupts the poller pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); long ms = (System.nanoTime() - asked) / 1_000_000; System.out.println(fixed ? "catch + restore the flag:" : "catch, swallowing:"); System.out.printf(" attempts before cancel: %d, after cancel: %d, shutdown took %d ms%n", cancelledAt, attempts.get() - cancelledAt, ms); } }

try.expect: Swallowing: 17 attempts after the cancel, and cancelAndJoin returns within a few milliseconds, because every remaining delay threw at once. Fixed: 0 attempts after the cancel. The swallowing Java twin also runs 17 more attempts, but over about 1.7 s: catching the interrupt cleared the flag, so the later sleeps were normal sleeps. Restoring the flag and returning stops it at once.

sections.h: A cancelled coroutine can't suspend, so cleanup needs NonCancellable
sections.html:
finally blocks run when a coroutine is cancelled, but they run inside a coroutine that is still cancelled. There, every suspension point throws CancellationException at once. Cleanup that suspends never gets past its first suspension:

Java
// Java equivalent: once the flag is set again, blocking cleanup fails at once
String hold = issuer.placeHold(amount);
try {
    awaitChallenge();
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();   // keep the cancel request, as you should
} finally {
    issuer.releaseHold(hold);             // blocks, sees the flag, throws InterruptedException
}
Kotlin
val hold = issuer.placeHold(amount)
try {
    awaitChallenge()             // cancelled here
} finally {
    issuer.releaseHold(hold)     // suspends, so it throws at once: the hold stays on the card
}

The fix is one wrapper: finally { withContext(NonCancellable) { issuer.releaseHold(hold) } }.

NonCancellable is a job that is always active. Inside that block, suspension points don't throw, so the release runs to the end. The coroutine itself stays cancelled. When the block finishes, the CancellationException carries on up the stack as before.

Use it in exactly this shape: withContext(NonCancellable), in a finally (or a cleanup catch), around the cleanup call and nothing else. The docs warn against launch(NonCancellable) or async(NonCancellable). Passing a job to a builder replaces the parent, so the new coroutine leaves the tree from lesson 3 of this track: nothing waits for it and nothing can cancel it. And keep the cleanup short. Nothing will cancel it for you, so give a slow network call its own withTimeout inside the block.

Cleanup that doesn't suspend needs nothing special. Closing a file, returning a JDBC connection to its pool, mutex.unlock() and semaphore.release() are ordinary calls and run fine in a cancelled coroutine.

The same rule explains a quieter loss. If a coroutine is cancelled while it waits for a call that returns a resource, such as a pooled session, it resumes with CancellationException even if the resource was already on its way. The resource is never handed to your code, so your code can't close it. Lesson 1 of this track showed the fix on the callback side: the onCancellation lambda of resume releases it.

try.title: Leave a hold on the card, then release it
steps: Read CleanupAfterCancel.kt. The payment is cancelled while it waits for a 3-D Secure challenge. Predict whether released hold-4250 prints.
Run it.
Run it with -Pargs=fixed, which wraps the release in withContext(NonCancellable).
Run the Java twin both ways.

code.title: CleanupAfterCancel.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l05 import kotlinx.coroutines.NonCancellable import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException private suspend fun releaseHold(id: String) { delay(50) // the network call to the issuer println(" released $id") } fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val fixed = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" val payment = launch { val hold = "hold-4250" println(" placed $hold") try { delay(10_000) // waiting for the customer's 3-D Secure challenge } finally { try { if (fixed) withContext(NonCancellable) { releaseHold(hold) } else releaseHold(hold) } catch (e: CancellationException) { println(" release failed at once: ${e::class.simpleName}") throw e } } } delay(100) println(if (fixed) "cancel, release inside withContext(NonCancellable):" else "cancel, plain suspend call in finally:") payment.cancelAndJoin() println(" payment job finished, cancelled = ${payment.isCancelled}") }

alt.title: CleanupAfterCancelJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of CleanupAfterCancel.kt: a thread that was interrupted can't make a blocking // cleanup call while its interrupt flag is set. Clear the flag for the cleanup, then restore it. package workbench.coroutines.l05; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class CleanupAfterCancelJava { static void releaseHold(String id) throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(50); // the network call to the issuer System.out.println(" released " + id); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean fixed = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); pool.submit(() -> { String hold = "hold-4250"; System.out.println(" placed " + hold); try { Thread.sleep(10_000); // waiting for the customer's 3-D Secure challenge } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // keep the cancel request, as you should } finally { boolean wasInterrupted = fixed && Thread.interrupted(); // fixed: clear the flag for cleanup try { releaseHold(hold); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println(" release failed at once: InterruptedException"); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } if (wasInterrupted) Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // and put it back afterwards } }); Thread.sleep(100); System.out.println(fixed ? "interrupt, flag cleared around the release:" : "interrupt, plain blocking call in finally:"); pool.shutdownNow(); pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.println(" task finished"); } }

try.expect: Without the wrapper, release failed at once: JobCancellationException prints, and the hold is never released. With -Pargs=fixed, released hold-4250 prints about 50 ms after the cancel, and the job still finishes as cancelled. The Java twin fails the same way with InterruptedException, and the fix there is to clear the flag around the cleanup and restore it afterwards.

sections.h: Timeouts are cancellation with a clock
sections.html:
withTimeout(d) { ... } runs the block and cancels it when d runs out. The cancellation is the ordinary kind: the block stops at its next suspension point, and withTimeout throws TimeoutCancellationException. withTimeoutOrNull(d) { ... } does the same and returns null instead of throwing.

Java
// Java equivalent: a fallback value when the future is late
Decision decision = issuer.authorizeAsync(request)
    .completeOnTimeout(Decision.TIMED_OUT, 800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
    .join();
Kotlin
val decision = withTimeoutOrNull(800.milliseconds) { issuer.authorize(request) }
    ?: Decision.TIMED_OUT          // decline, or route to the fallback acquirer

Prefer withTimeoutOrNull when a timeout is an outcome you expect. TimeoutCancellationException is a subclass of CancellationException, and that has a surprising effect. Inside launch, a timeout looks like an ordinary cancel, so the docs' own pitfall applies: a child that times out inside coroutineScope lets the scope finish normally, and nobody hears about it. If a timeout should fail the caller, turn it into a real error: withTimeoutOrNull(d) { ... } ?: error("issuer timed out").

A timeout is still cooperative, so it can't stop a blocking call. A thread blocked in Thread.sleep, a socket read or a JDBC call is not at a suspension point. withTimeout(300) { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { client.lookup(bin) } } waits for the whole call and only then throws, and the IO thread stays busy the whole time. If the blocking call is the entire block, with no suspension at all, the timeout is ignored and the late result comes back as if nothing had happened.

For blocking code that responds to interrupts, use runInterruptible:

Java
// Java equivalent: give up after the timeout and interrupt the worker
Future<String> f = io.submit(() -> binDirectory.lookup(bin));
try { return f.get(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); }
catch (TimeoutException e) { f.cancel(true); return null; }   // interrupts the blocked thread
Kotlin
withTimeoutOrNull(300.milliseconds) {
    runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { binDirectory.lookup(bin) }   // interrupted on cancel
}

runInterruptible runs the block on the dispatcher you give it. When the coroutine is cancelled, it interrupts that thread, and it turns the resulting InterruptedException back into a CancellationException. It only helps if the blocking call responds to interrupts. Thread.sleep, BlockingQueue.take and java.nio interruptible channels do. A classic socket read on a platform thread doesn't, and JDBC drivers vary, so set the client's own timeout too.

try.title: Time out a slow issuer four ways
steps: Read TimeoutsAndBlocking.kt. The issuer takes 1.5 s and every call gets 300 ms. Predict the outcome and the time for each line.
Run it.
Delete the withContext(Dispatchers.IO) wrapper in the third case, leaving withTimeout(300) { Thread.sleep(1_500); "approved" }. Predict, then run.
Run the Java twin and compare orTimeout with get plus cancel(true).

code.title: TimeoutsAndBlocking.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l05 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.TimeoutCancellationException import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.runInterruptible import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeout import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull /** Runs [block] and prints what came out and how long it took. */ private suspend fun timed(label: String, block: suspend () -> Any?) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val outcome = try { "returned ${block()}" } catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) { "threw TimeoutCancellationException" } println("%-50s %-36s after %5d ms".format(label, outcome, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) } fun main() = runBlocking { // the issuer takes 1.5 s; we give it 300 ms timed("withTimeout { delay }") { withTimeout(300) { delay(1_500); "approved" } } timed("withTimeoutOrNull { delay }") { withTimeoutOrNull(300) { delay(1_500); "approved" } } timed("withTimeout { withContext(IO) { sleep } }") { withTimeout(300) { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { Thread.sleep(1_500); "approved" } } } timed("withTimeoutOrNull { runInterruptible { sleep } }") { withTimeoutOrNull(300) { runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { Thread.sleep(1_500); "approved" } } } }

alt.title: TimeoutsAndBlockingJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of TimeoutsAndBlocking.kt: a timeout on a CompletableFuture gives the caller // an answer on time, but nothing stops the blocking task. Future.cancel(true) interrupts it. package workbench.coroutines.l05; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; public class TimeoutsAndBlockingJava { static long t0; static String callIssuer() { try { Thread.sleep(1_500); // the issuer takes 1.5 s System.out.printf(" (the issuer call itself finished at %d ms)%n", ms()); return "approved"; } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.printf(" (the issuer call was interrupted at %d ms)%n", ms()); return "interrupted"; } } static long ms() { return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newCachedThreadPool()) { // 1. orTimeout: the caller gets a TimeoutException on time, the task runs on t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(TimeoutsAndBlockingJava::callIssuer, io).orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { System.out.printf("orTimeout(300 ms) caller got %s after %d ms%n", e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName(), ms()); } Thread.sleep(1_400); // wait, to see the abandoned task finish anyway // 2. Future.get with a timeout, then cancel(true): the blocked thread is interrupted t0 = System.nanoTime(); Future<String> f = io.submit(TimeoutsAndBlockingJava::callIssuer); try { f.get(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } catch (TimeoutException e) { f.cancel(true); System.out.printf("get(300 ms) + cancel(true) caller gave up after %d ms%n", ms()); } Thread.sleep(100); } } }

try.expect: The two delay cases end at about 300 ms: one throws, one returns null. The withContext(IO) case throws too, but only after about 1,500 ms, when the sleep is over. runInterruptible returns null at about 300 ms. After your change, the bare sleep returns approved after 1,500 ms: the block never suspended, so the timeout was ignored. In the Java twin, orTimeout gives the caller its exception on time while the abandoned call finishes at 1,500 ms anyway; cancel(true) interrupts it at about 300 ms.

analogy: Cancelling a coroutine is like a manager putting a "stop, we're closing" note on each worker's desk. A worker who looks up between tasks (a suspension point) sees it, tidies up and goes home. A worker deep in a long calculation who never looks up keeps going until the calculation is done. A worker on hold with a supplier (a blocking call) can't see the desk at all until someone taps them on the shoulder, which is what runInterruptible does. runCatching is the worker who reads the note, throws it in the bin and starts the next task. NonCancellable is the exemption for tidying up: "finish putting the cash in the safe, then go." The analogy breaks in one place: binning the note doesn't make it go away. Every desk the worker sits at afterwards has the same note on it.
world: Cancellation reaches your payment code more often than you think. A Kafka rebalance revokes a partition, and its worker's scope is cancelled. A Quarkus shutdown cancels long-lived scopes in @PreDestroy. Every withTimeout on an issuer call is a cancel waiting to happen. Three things keep that safe. Never wrap a suspend call in runCatching or catch (e: Exception) without rethrowing CancellationException, or a shutdown turns into a list of fake failures. Release card holds, distributed locks and idempotency claims in finally with withContext(NonCancellable). And remember that an Oracle query running in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) ignores the timeout around it: use runInterruptible only if the driver responds to interrupts, and set Statement.setQueryTimeout either way. Temporal works on the same idea: an activity learns that it has been cancelled only when it heartbeats.
mistake: The most common mistake is swallowing CancellationException with a catch-all: runCatching { }, catch (e: Exception) or catch (e: Throwable) around a suspend call, usually written to "log and keep going" in a batch or polling loop. It looks like good defensive code, and it works perfectly until the first shutdown or timeout. Then the loop either reports every remaining item as failed or spins at full CPU, and a cancelled job seems to hang or to finish with nonsense. The fix: rethrow CancellationException before handling anything else (if (e is CancellationException) throw e), or catch only the exception types you expect from the call.

compare.title: Stopping a CPU loop: Future.cancel(true) vs Job.cancel()

java.title: ReconciliationJob.java
java.html: Future<Integer> f = pool.submit(() -> { int matched = 0; for (int i = 0; i < entries.size(); i++) { if (i % 1_000 == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { throw new CancellationException("reconciliation stopped at " + i); // 1. look at the flag } if (matches(entries.get(i))) matched++; } return matched; }); f.cancel(true); // 2. sets the worker's interrupt flag; the loop stops at its next check

kotlin.title: ReconciliationJob.kt
kotlin.html: val job = scope.async(Dispatchers.Default) { var matched = 0 for ((i, entry) in entries.withIndex()) { if (i % 1_000 == 0) ensureActive() // 1. throws CancellationException once cancelled if (matches(entry)) matched++ } matched } job.cancel() // 2. marks the job cancelled; the loop stops at its next check

compare.note: Both models are cooperative, and both loops need the same explicit check. The differences are in what carries the request. Java's interrupt is a flag on a thread. Catching InterruptedException clears it, so a swallowed interrupt is lost, and the request doesn't reach other threads the task started. A coroutine's cancellation is a state on its job. It stays set, it flows down to every child in the tree, and every suspension point checks it. The two also see different things: blocking JDK calls react to interrupts but not to job cancellation (bridge them with runInterruptible), while suspension points react to job cancellation and ignore the interrupt flag.

worked.title: Make a chargeback poller stop cleanly

steps.say: A poller checks a chargeback's status every 5 s until the card scheme decides. It holds a lease (a row lock in Oracle) so only one pod polls each case. During a deploy, pods take 30 s to shut down, and leases stay locked until they expire. Find the three problems before reading on.
steps.code: suspend fun pollChargeback(id: String): Status { val lease = leases.acquire(id) try { while (true) { try { val s = scheme.status(id) if (s.isFinal) return s delay(5.seconds) } catch (e: Exception) { log.warn("poll failed for $id", e) } } } finally { leases.release(lease) // suspend: a network call to Oracle } }

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the same bugs Status pollChargeback(String id) { Lease lease = leases.acquire(id); try { while (true) { try { Status s = scheme.status(id); if (s.isFinal()) return s; Thread.sleep(5_000); } catch (Exception e) { // also catches InterruptedException log.warn("poll failed for {}", id, e); } } } finally { leases.release(lease); // fails at once if the flag is set } }

steps.say: Problem 1: catch (e: Exception) swallows the CancellationException from delay, so a cancelled poller spins. Catch only the scheme client's error, and let cancellation through.
steps.code: while (true) { try { val s = scheme.status(id) if (s.isFinal) return s } catch (e: SchemeException) { // 1. only what we expect from the call log.warn("poll failed for $id", e) } delay(5.seconds) // outside the try: a cancel ends the loop }

alt.html: while (true) { try { Status s = scheme.status(id); if (s.isFinal()) return s; } catch (SchemeException e) { // 1. only what we expect from the call log.warn("poll failed for {}", id, e); } Thread.sleep(5_000); // InterruptedException now propagates }

steps.say: Problem 2: the lease release suspends in a cancelled coroutine, so it throws before it reaches Oracle. Wrap it in NonCancellable, with its own short timeout so a stuck database can't hold up shutdown.
steps.code: } finally { // 2. cleanup that suspends must run non-cancellable, and bounded withContext(NonCancellable) { withTimeoutOrNull(2.seconds) { leases.release(lease) } } }

alt.html: } finally { // 2. clear the flag for the cleanup, then restore it boolean interrupted = Thread.interrupted(); try { leases.release(lease); } finally { if (interrupted) Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }

steps.say: Problem 3: nothing bounds the whole poll. Give the caller a deadline, and treat running out as an expected outcome rather than an exception.
steps.code: // 3. the caller decides how long a poll may take val status: Status? = withTimeoutOrNull(10.minutes) { pollChargeback(id) } if (status == null) scheduleRetry(id) // still undecided: try again from the outbox later

alt.html: // 3. the caller decides how long a poll may take Future<Status> f = pool.submit(() -> pollChargeback(id)); try { handle(f.get(10, TimeUnit.MINUTES)); } catch (TimeoutException e) { f.cancel(true); scheduleRetry(id); }

steps.say: Self-check: the timeout in step 3 cancels pollChargeback while it is suspended in delay. Trace what happens. (The delay throws TimeoutCancellationException, it passes the narrow catch, the finally releases the lease under NonCancellable, and withTimeoutOrNull turns the exception into null.)

lab.title: Fix four cancellation bugs in a payments batch
steps: Run the tests. Four of eight fail, one per file. Each stub is the buggy code, and its KDoc says what is wrong.
FraudScan.kt: make countFlagged check for cancellation at least once every 1,000 amounts.
SettlementRun.kt: keep runCatching, but make a CancellationException end the run instead of being logged as a failed batch.
CardHold.kt: make the release in finally run to the end even when the caller was cancelled.
BinLookup.kt: return null on timeout instead of throwing, and make the timeout interrupt the blocked lookup call.
Run the tests until all eight pass, then run them once more.
hints: countFlagged is a plain suspend function with no scope receiver, so call currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive(). Read the context once, before the loop.
Import CancellationException from kotlin.coroutines.cancellation (or kotlinx.coroutines). Both name the same class.
The release fix is one wrapper: withContext(NonCancellable) { ... }.
runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { ... } replaces withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { ... } for blocking code that should be interrupted on cancel.
lab.done: All eight tests in CancellationTest pass, twice in a row.

drill.title: A cancellable batch from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write suspend fun reprice(rows: List<Row>, lease: Lease) that runs on Dispatchers.Default, checks for cancellation every 500 rows, calls price(row) (which can throw PricingException; log and skip the row), and always releases the lease with the suspending lease.release(), even after a cancel.

answer.html: suspend fun reprice(rows: List<Row>, lease: Lease) { try { withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { for ((i, row) in rows.withIndex()) { if (i % 500 == 0) ensureActive() // cooperate with cancel try { price(row) } catch (e: PricingException) { // only what we expect log.warn("skipping ${row.id}", e) } } } } finally { withContext(NonCancellable) { lease.release() } // suspending cleanup } }

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent: read the interrupt flag, clear it around the cleanup void reprice(List<Row> rows, Lease lease) { try { for (int i = 0; i < rows.size(); i++) { if (i % 500 == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) return; // cooperate with cancel try { price(rows.get(i)); } catch (PricingException e) { // only what we expect log.warn("skipping {}", rows.get(i).id(), e); } } } finally { boolean interrupted = Thread.interrupted(); try { lease.release(); } // blocking cleanup finally { if (interrupted) Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

recap: Cancellation is cooperative. cancel() marks the job, and the coroutine stops at its next suspension point or explicit check. CPU loops need ensureActive(), isActive or yield().
Cancellation travels as CancellationException. runCatching, catch (e: Exception) and catch (e: Throwable) all catch it, so rethrow it or catch narrower types.
In a cancelled coroutine every suspension point throws at once. Run suspending cleanup in finally inside withContext(NonCancellable), and never pass NonCancellable to launch or async.
withTimeout throws TimeoutCancellationException (a CancellationException), and withTimeoutOrNull returns null. Inside launch, a timeout doesn't fail the parent unless you turn it into an error.
Timeouts can't stop blocking calls. Wrap interruptible blocking code in runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO), and give clients such as JDBC their own timeouts.
flow { } checks for cancellation on each emit; asFlow() doesn't, so add .cancellable().

explain.prompt: A teammate wrapped every call in a settlement loop in runCatching "so one bad batch never stops the run". After the last deploy, the shutdown logs listed forty failed batches that had never failed. Explain what happened and how you'd change the code.
explain.answer: When the pod shut down, the settlement coroutine was cancelled. Cancellation reaches the code as a CancellationException thrown from the next suspension point, and runCatching catches every Throwable, so it caught that too and logged the batch in progress as failed. The coroutine was still cancelled, so the next batch threw at its first suspension point, got caught and logged the same way, and so on through all forty remaining batches. Then the function returned normally. I'd keep the per-batch error handling but rethrow CancellationException before logging anything, or catch only the exceptions the settle call is expected to throw. Then a cancel ends the run at the batch in progress, and any cleanup that suspends goes in a finally inside withContext(NonCancellable).

deeper.html:
A CancellationException doesn't always mean "I was cancelled". If you await() a Deferred that someone else cancelled, await throws CancellationException in your coroutine, even though your coroutine is fine. The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 KDoc calls this out as a legacy behavior that can't be changed compatibly: your coroutine then ends as "cancelled", so its parent isn't told and the work silently stops. If you catch it, check currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() in the catch. It throws only if your coroutine was cancelled, so after it you know the exception came from the thing you awaited, and you can turn it into a real error.

The library also gives a prompt cancellation guarantee. If a coroutine is cancelled while suspended, it resumes with CancellationException even when the value it was waiting for had already arrived. withContext checks for cancellation both on entry and when its block returns. So val conn = withContext(io) { pool.borrow() } can lose a connection: the block borrowed it, the caller was cancelled in the meantime, and the result is thrown away. Borrow and release inside the same block, or use the onCancellation callback of CancellableContinuation.resume when you write the bridge yourself (lesson 1 of this track).

Timeouts have one more subtle rule. The KDoc says cancellation on timeout "may happen at any time, even after the block finishes executing but before the caller gets resumed". So never write withTimeout { resource = open() } and expect resource to be either unset or yours. Open the resource outside the timeout, or close it in the block's own finally.

Finally, runBlocking bridges in the other direction. If the thread blocked in runBlocking is interrupted, the coroutine is cancelled and runBlocking throws InterruptedException. That is how a coroutine-based Kafka handler called from a plain consumer thread can still be stopped by shutdownNow().
